chapter_theme: The conduct of Brahmins (அந்தணர் ஒழுக்கம்): a Brahmin is one who keeps the rites and through them reaches Vedanta, where craving ends; thread, tuft and birth without truth, knowledge and devotion don't make one.
structure_note: 224 to 227 describe the Brahmin by rite, mantra and Pranava; 228 to 233 redefine him by truth, freedom from craving and knowledge, with thread and tuft dismissed in 230 and the rites left behind in 232; 234 to 237 give the fruits for land, king and release.

224.reading: Brahmins are those who keep the six duties, tend the red fire, keep the rules at the three times of day, stand in good works, recite the twilight prayers, and so cut away ritual.
224.nuance: சடங்கறுப்போர் can mean those who complete the rites or those who end them; the second fits 232, where the rites are set aside, but the line doesn't settle it. The six duties are traditionally learning and teaching the Veda, sacrificing and having others sacrifice, giving and receiving.

225.reading: Brahmins are those who, eager to hear Vedanta, enter the Pranava in which the three states of knowing end, and see with joy the Lord who is the end of sound, of the Veda and of knowledge, without fixing any one thing as that end.
225.nuance: The verse stacks technical 'ends': நாதாந்தம் (end of sound), வேதாந்தம் (end of the Veda), போதாந்தம் (end of knowing). முப்பதம் may be the three letters of Om or three states. ஈதாந்தம் எனாது, 'not saying this is the end', refuses to stop at any one of them.

226.reading: The Vedic Brahmins are those glad to study the Gayatri and Savitri, who meditate on the mantra, ride the chariot of love into steady thought, and, become love itself, are not drowned in maya.
226.nuance: நேயம் (love, devotion) appears twice: as the chariot one rides and as what one becomes. The verse makes devotion the means of reciting the mantra rightly.

227.reading: The faultless Brahmins are those who grasp the Pranava, the great path, join the word through the guru's way, keep to the rites of the four Vedas, and become one with the true form.
227.nuance: சொரூபம், 'own form', is taken as the soul's true nature or Siva's; the verse doesn't say which.

228.reading: Truthfulness, austerity, becoming one with Him, wearing down the craving senses, knowing all lives as equal to oneself, and cutting off bondage: this is Brahman.
228.nuance: The verse defines பிரமம், the Brahmin's own word, by conduct. தானவன் ஆதலும் could be 'becoming He' or 'being a giver'; I take the first. ஒத்த உயிர்கள் means all lives seen as alike.

229.reading: Brahmins eager to hear Vedanta heard it and still kept their craving; but Vedanta is where craving ends, so those who have truly heard it have let craving go.
229.nuance: The verse plays வேதாந்தம் against வேட்கை (craving): the end of the Veda is the end of wanting. Hearing that leaves craving intact wasn't hearing.

230.reading: Are the sacred thread and the tuft Brahman? The thread is cotton and the tuft is hair; the real thread is Vedanta and the real tuft knowledge, as thread-wearing Brahmins would see if they looked.
230.nuance: The verse doesn't tell Brahmins to drop the thread; it says what the thread stands for. 241 goes further.

231.reading: Those mad fools without truth, without knowledge, without the sense that turns from the objects of the senses, without devotion and without knowing the Supreme are not Brahmins.
231.nuance: Five absences are listed and none of them is birth, so the verse denies the name to the born Brahmin who lacks them.

232.reading: For pure Brahmins, turiya samadhi is reaching the guru's feet by the guru's way, beyond the division of the conscious and the inert, and seeing once the rites and rules have been set aside.
232.nuance: துரியம் is the fourth state beyond waking, dream and deep sleep; சித்தசித்து is the conscious and the inert. These are Siddhanta and Vedanta terms whose exact sense here I can't fix. The verse places the rites of 224 below the goal.

233.reading: Brahmins are truly such when their purity comes from the truth of Vedanta; knowing that what lacks it is mere noise, they know the Veda and are Brahmins.
233.nuance: The grammar of the second and third lines is loose; I take கோலாகலம் (noise, show) as the verdict on rite without Vedanta.

234.reading: The fertile land where Brahmins who wear cool kindness and meditate on the end of the Veda live does not decline and its king prospers; they make the oblation at dusk and dawn.
234.nuance: அந்தண்மை பூண்ட echoes the Kural's செந்தண்மை பூண்டொழுகலான் (Kural 30), the edition's own parallel. Here the Brahmin's virtue benefits the land and king.

235.reading: For those whose rule makes the knowledge of Vedanta shine, the course that approaches the awareness at the end of sound enters the Supreme beyond knowing, and so both release at the end of sound and powers are reached.
235.nuance: Again the verse stacks Vedanta, நாதாந்தம் and போதாந்தம், as technical stages. It promises both முத்தி (release) and சித்தி (powers) without ranking them.

236.reading: When the one and the two are brought together, those blessed with grace, however well they live and however many good things they speak, seek out and go to worship the Lord who shines victorious.
236.nuance: ஒன்றும் இரண்டும் is unexplained: it could be the soul and Siva, the self and its two bonds, or a number of breaths or syllables. The rest of the verse is clear: worship remains even for the accomplished.

237.reading: When the two attachments fall away of themselves, the self is let go and nothing is sought; then Brahma on his flower, enjoying merit, receives the single oblation of Om.
237.nuance: The two attachments are traditionally 'I' and 'mine'. The verse seems to make the giving up of self the true oblation, received by the gods; the third and fourth lines are hard to construe.

links.note: Both define the Brahmin's state by regard for every living being: the Kural's அந்தணர் are clothed in kindness to all lives, Tirumular's Brahman includes knowing all lives as one's equal.
Both define the goal by the end of craving: the Kural says the freed are those freed of craving, Tirumular that Vedanta is the place where craving ends.
Both deny that marks of the body make the holy man: the Kural says neither shaving nor long hair is needed, Tirumular that the thread is cotton and the tuft hair.
Both make the Brahmin depend on conduct, not birth: the Kural says his birth is ruined when conduct declines, Tirumular denies the name to those without truth and knowledge.
Tirumular's அந்தண்மை பூண்ட echoes the Kural's செந்தண்மை பூண்டு: both define the அந்தணர் by a coolness of heart they wear. Tirumular adds that the land where they live prospers.
If the two attachments are 'I' and 'mine', both say cutting them raises one above the gods: the Kural to a world higher than theirs, Tirumular to an offering they receive.
224 defines Brahmins by the daily rites; 232 makes the highest state one reached once the rites are set aside, so the rites are a stage, not the goal.

225 says true Brahmins enter the Pranava and see the Lord who is the end of sound, Veda and knowing (நாதாந்த வேதாந்த போதாந்த நாதனை). 2386, in the chapter on the six ends, sets these ends out together: Vedanta and Siddhanta a single seal, bodhanta, yoganta and nadanta becoming bliss in the silence (மோனத்து மூழ்கவே). The terms named in passing in the Brahmins' chapter are given their full scheme later in the book.

227 says faultless Brahmins grasp the Pranava, join the word by the guru's way (குருநெறியால்) and keep to the rites of the four Vedas (நால்வேதத் திருநெறியான கிரியை இருந்து). 232 takes the same guru's way (குருநெறியாலே) further: turiya samadhi comes when rites and rules are let go (கரும நியமாதி கைவிட்டு). Read together, the rites 227 requires are a stage that 232 says is left behind.

235 says that for those in whom Vedanta knowledge shines, the course toward the awareness at the end of sound reaches the Supreme and gains release at the end of sound (நாதாந்த முத்தி). 2821 says the good path of knowledge is the good path of nadanta and its release is the Veda of nadanta (ஞானத்தின் நன்மோக நாதாந்த வேதமே). Both place release at nadanta and bind it to knowledge.
